cards.front: What five groups benefited most from the 1920s economic boom?
cards.answer: Businessmen and industrialists / Workers in new industries / City dwellers / Stock market speculators / Middle-class families

cards.front: What five groups were left behind by the 1920s boom?
cards.answer: Farmers / African Americans / Native Americans / Workers in old industries / Recent immigrants

cards.front: Why did farm incomes collapse in the 1920s?
cards.answer: Farmers expanded production during the war to feed Europe, but demand fell afterwards, causing overproduction and collapsing crop prices.

cards.front: Why was Ford able to cut the price of the Model T?
cards.answer: Ford standardised the Model T — one colour, one engine — so fewer skilled workers were needed, cutting production costs.

cards.front: What four areas of change for women went beyond the flapper image in the 1920s?
cards.answer: Employment / New technology in the home / Birth control / Education

cards.front: What five limits does this lesson give on women's progress in the 1920s?
cards.answer: Rural vs urban divide / Race / Class / Political impact / Backlash

cards.front: How did the First World War change job opportunities for American women?
cards.answer: With millions of men away fighting, women took on new jobs in factories, offices and farms, gaining independence and confidence.

cards.front: Why did many rural, religious Americans oppose the flapper lifestyle?
cards.answer: They saw flappers' drinking, dancing and immodest fashion as sinful and a threat to traditional values.

cards.front: What four reasons does this lesson give for the introduction of Prohibition?
cards.answer: The temperance movement / Religious and moral arguments / Industrial efficiency / Anti-German sentiment

cards.front: What four criminal activities earned Al Capone's gang its fortune?
cards.answer: Bootlegging / Gambling dens / Brothels / Protection rackets

cards.front: Why did ending Prohibition benefit the American economy?
cards.answer: It created jobs, brought in tax revenue, and cut off a major income source for organised crime.

cards.front: Why did some poor Americans see Al Capone as a 'Robin Hood' figure?
cards.answer: He opened soup kitchens to feed the homeless when the Depression began, despite his crimes.

cards.front: What four reasons does this lesson give for growing hostility towards immigrants in the 1920s?
cards.answer: Competition for jobs / Cultural fears / The Red Scare / Racism

cards.front: What three symbols did the revived Ku Klux Klan keep from the original Klan?
cards.answer: White robes / Hoods / Burning crosses

cards.front: Why did the 1924 National Origins Act base its quotas on the 1890 census?
cards.answer: The 1890 census predated the surge of Southern and Eastern European immigrants, so quotas favoured Northern and Western Europeans instead.

cards.front: Why did many believe Sacco and Vanzetti were wrongly convicted?
cards.answer: Many believed they were convicted for being Italian immigrants and anarchists, not because of the weak evidence against them.

cards.front: What three 'Black' days marked the Wall Street Crash of October 1929?
cards.answer: Black Thursday (24 Oct) / Black Monday (28 Oct) / Black Tuesday (29 Oct)

cards.front: What four immediate consequences did the Wall Street Crash have on the economy?
cards.answer: Investors ruined / Banks collapsed / Businesses failed / Unemployment soared

cards.front: Why did American factories overproduce goods in the late 1920s?
cards.answer: Mass production created goods faster than wages rose, so ordinary workers could not afford to buy enough to match it.

cards.front: Why did buying shares 'on the margin' ruin investors when the market crashed?
cards.answer: Margin buyers paid only around 10% upfront with borrowed money, so falling prices left them owing more than their shares were worth.

cards.front: What three causes does this lesson give for the Dust Bowl?
cards.answer: Over-farming / Drought / Dust storms

cards.front: What five groups' experiences during the Depression does this lesson describe?
cards.answer: African Americans / Hispanic Americans / Women / Children / Farmers

cards.front: Why was Hoover's Reconstruction Finance Corporation criticised?
cards.answer: Critics said it helped the rich — 'feeding the sparrows by feeding the horse' — while ordinary people kept starving.

cards.front: Why did the Bonus Army march on Washington in 1932?
cards.answer: Unemployed First World War veterans demanded early payment of a war service bonus that was not due until 1945.

cards.front: What three things did the Social Security Act of 1935 create?
cards.answer: A pension for over-65s / Unemployment insurance / Help for disabled people and mothers
items: Help for disabled people and mothers

cards.front: What five limitations does this lesson give for the New Deal?
cards.answer: Did not end the Depression / Did little for African Americans / Jobs mostly designed for men / Left huge government debt / Did not fix the economic system
items: Did not fix the economic system

cards.front: Why is the Tennessee Valley Authority often seen as the most successful New Deal programme?
cards.answer: It built 21 dams that controlled flooding, generated cheap power, and brought electricity to a poor rural region for the first time.

cards.front: Why was Roosevelt's 1937 'court-packing' plan controversial?
cards.answer: Even his own supporters saw it as an attempt to undermine the Supreme Court's independence, and Congress rejected the plan.

title: The Impact of World War Two

cards.front: What four things did American factories produce in huge numbers during World War Two?
cards.answer: 300,000 aircraft / 86,000 tanks / 2.5 million trucks / 6,500 naval vessels

cards.front: What three benefits did the 1944 GI Bill provide to returning veterans?
cards.answer: College or vocational education / Low-cost home loans / Unemployment insurance

cards.front: Why could many African American veterans not benefit equally from the GI Bill?
cards.answer: Racist banks often denied them home loans, and many white universities, especially in the South, refused to admit them.

cards.front: Why did World War Two succeed in ending the Great Depression where the New Deal had not?
cards.answer: Massive wartime government spending on war production created millions of jobs, finally achieving full employment.

cards.front: What five reasons does this lesson give for the post-war economic boom?
cards.answer: Wartime production / Pent-up demand / Government spending / New technology / Population growth

cards.front: What four groups or problems does this lesson say were left behind by post-war prosperity?
cards.answer: African Americans / Inner-city poverty / Rural poverty / Conformity and discontent

cards.front: Why were suburbs like Levittown overwhelmingly white?
cards.answer: Levittown's contracts explicitly banned sales to African Americans, and banks 'redlined' Black neighbourhoods, trapping Black families in declining inner cities.

cards.front: Why did rock and roll create a 'generation gap' between teenagers and their parents?
cards.answer: Adults criticised it for encouraging rebellion, sexual freedom and disrespect for authority, while teenagers embraced it as their own culture.

cards.front: What six ways does this lesson say McCarthyism damaged American civil liberties?
cards.answer: Freedom of speech restricted / Freedom of association restricted / Due process undermined / Careers destroyed by accusation / The McCarran Internal Security Act / Chilling effect on reform

cards.front: Why was Alger Hiss convicted of perjury rather than espionage?
cards.answer: The statute of limitations meant he could not be charged with espionage, so he was convicted of perjury for lying under oath.

cards.front: Why did Senator McCarthy's power collapse in 1954?
cards.answer: Televised hearings showed him bullying witnesses; after lawyer Joseph Welch publicly exposed him, the Senate voted to censure him.

cards.front: What three things did the Little Rock crisis show, according to this lesson?
cards.answer: Southern states would use force to resist / The federal government could be pressured into acting / Media coverage was a powerful weapon
items: Southern states would use force to resist
The federal government could be pressured into acting
Media coverage was a powerful weapon

cards.front: What five limitations does this lesson give on the impact of Brown v. Board of Education?
cards.answer: No deadline was set for desegregation / Many Southern states refused to comply / White Citizens' Councils fought integration / No integrated schools in some states by 1957 / It applied only to schools
items: No deadline was set for desegregation
Many Southern states refused to comply
No integrated schools in some states by 1957

cards.front: Why did the NAACP shift its strategy towards fighting segregation through the courts?
cards.answer: The federal government refused to challenge Southern politicians over 'states' rights', so the NAACP brought carefully chosen test cases to court instead.

cards.front: Why did the NAACP build its Montgomery bus case around Rosa Parks rather than Claudette Colvin?
cards.answer: Colvin was a pregnant teenager, seen as an unsympathetic figure, so the NAACP chose the more respectable, experienced Rosa Parks instead.

title: Civil Rights: King, Malcolm X & Black Power

cards.front: What four causes does this lesson give for the mid-1960s urban riots in Northern cities?
cards.answer: Poverty / Poor housing / Unemployment / Police brutality

cards.front: Why did King's Birmingham campaign succeed where the earlier Albany campaign had failed?
cards.answer: King chose Birmingham because its commissioner, Bull Connor, was certain to react with visible violence, generating the media coverage Albany lacked.

cards.front: Why did Malcolm X's message appeal to young Black Americans in Northern cities?
cards.answer: Legal segregation did not exist there, but poverty, unemployment and police brutality still fuelled deep frustration among young Black residents.

cards.front: What five areas did Kennedy's New Frontier propose reforms in?
cards.answer: Healthcare / Education / Poverty / Housing / Civil rights

cards.front: What four criticisms did conservatives make of Johnson's Great Society?
cards.answer: Created welfare dependency / Government grew too large / Funded radical activist groups / Did not tackle root causes of poverty
items: Did not tackle root causes of poverty

cards.front: Why did the Vietnam War undermine Johnson's Great Society programmes?
cards.answer: As the war's cost soared, Johnson had to choose between funding it and his domestic programmes, and Vietnam spending won.

cards.front: Why did Johnson achieve far more than Kennedy despite continuing much of his agenda?
cards.answer: Johnson was a master of congressional politics with a landslide election mandate, while Kennedy faced a hostile Congress and a short time in office.

cards.front: What five arguments did Phyllis Schlafly use against the Equal Rights Amendment?
cards.answer: Force women into combat / End separate toilets for men and women / Remove divorce protections like alimony / Undermine the traditional family / Lead to taxpayer-funded abortion
items: End separate toilets for men and women

cards.front: What four reasons does this lesson give for the Equal Rights Amendment's failure?
cards.answer: Schlafly's campaign frightened many women / Seen as representing only middle-class white women / Opposition from religious conservatives / The broader conservative backlash of the late 1970s
items: Seen as representing only middle-class white women
The broader conservative backlash of the late 1970s

cards.front: Why was the word 'sex' added to Title VII of the 1964 Civil Rights Act?
cards.answer: A Southern congressman, Howard Smith, added the word hoping it would make the whole bill fail, but it passed anyway.

cards.front: Why did Betty Friedan and others found NOW in 1966?
cards.answer: The EEOC was not enforcing Title VII's ban on sex discrimination seriously, so Friedan and others founded NOW to fight for change.

cards.front: What five themes does this lesson identify running across the whole America unit?
cards.answer: Opportunity vs inequality / The role of government / The power of protest / Ideals vs reality / The limits of law

cards.front: What four deep inequalities does this lesson say persisted in America by 1973?
cards.answer: De facto segregation in housing and jobs / Vast racial and gender economic inequality / The ERA failed and pay gaps stayed wide / The American Dream stayed unfulfilled for millions
items: De facto segregation in housing and jobs
Vast racial and gender economic inequality
The ERA failed and pay gaps stayed wide
The American Dream stayed unfulfilled for millions

cards.front: Why does this lesson argue that passing laws alone could not achieve real equality?
cards.answer: Laws banned discrimination but could not by themselves change attitudes, economic structures and institutions, which real equality also needed.

cards.front: Why does this lesson call America's progress between 1920 and 1973 'unfinished business'?
cards.answer: Legal rights were won on paper, but turning them into genuine equality of opportunity and outcome remained incomplete.

cards.front: What five issues did the Big Three disagree on at the Paris Peace Conference?
cards.answer: Land / Reparations and trade / The League of Nations / Disarmament / Self-determination

cards.front: What were the first five of Wilson's Fourteen Points?
cards.answer: No secret treaties / Free access to the seas / Free trade between countries / Disarmament by all countries / Colonies to have a say in their future
items: Colonies to have a say in their future

cards.front: Why was applying self-determination in Eastern Europe so difficult?
cards.answer: Ethnic groups there were hopelessly mixed together, so borders could not follow ethnic lines cleanly, leaving many Germans outside Germany.

cards.front: Why did Wilson compromise on many of his Fourteen Points at the peace conference?
cards.answer: He gave up many of his ideals in order to secure the one thing he cared about most: the League of Nations.

cards.front: What four main areas did the Treaty of Versailles punish Germany across?
cards.answer: Military terms / Territorial terms / Economic terms / Article 231 (War Guilt Clause)

cards.front: Why did the Treaty's separate terms make Germany's situation worse than any single term alone?
cards.answer: Losing industrial regions made reparations harder to pay, and forced coal deliveries and military restrictions left Germany unable to resist.

cards.front: Why did the War Guilt Clause anger Germans so much?
cards.answer: Germans did not believe they alone caused the war, having been told by propaganda that they were fighting a defensive war.

cards.front: What five grievances does this lesson list for Germany against the Treaty?
cards.answer: The War Guilt Clause / Reparations of £6.6 billion / Territorial losses / Military restrictions / Exclusion from the talks

cards.front: What five reasons does the 'U BRAT' mnemonic give for why Germany hated the Treaty of Versailles?
cards.answer: Unfair (Diktat) / Blame (War Guilt Clause) / Reparations (£6.6 billion) / Army (100,000 limit) / Territory (10% of land lost)

cards.front: Why did Germany suffer hyperinflation in 1923?
cards.answer: France invaded the Ruhr after a missed reparations payment; workers struck, and the government printed worthless money to pay them anyway.

cards.front: Why did right-wing politicians spread the 'stab in the back' myth about the Treaty?
cards.answer: They had resigned before the signing, letting the new government take the blame, then used the myth to attack it for years.

cards.front: What three problems does this lesson identify with the new states created after the First World War?
cards.answer: Minority populations under foreign rule / Economic weakness / Political instability

cards.front: What five peace treaties, besides Versailles, made up the wider WWI peace settlement?
cards.answer: Treaty of St Germain (Austria) / Treaty of Neuilly (Bulgaria) / Treaty of Trianon (Hungary) / Treaty of Sèvres (Turkey) / Treaty of Lausanne (Turkey, revised)

cards.front: Why did Turkey get a fairer treaty (Lausanne) than the other defeated nations?
cards.answer: Turkish nationalist forces under Atatürk fought back and reclaimed lost territory, forcing the Allies to negotiate a fairer replacement treaty.

cards.front: Why were the Big Three under time pressure during the peace negotiations?
cards.answer: Allied armies were demobilising after 1918, so the longer talks dragged on, the weaker their bargaining position became.

cards.front: What four aims did the League of Nations have?
cards.answer: Stop war through collective security / Improve lives and working conditions / Achieve disarmament / Enforce the Treaty of Versailles

cards.front: What were the three steps of collective security under the League's Covenant?
cards.answer: Moral condemnation / Economic sanctions / Military force

cards.front: Why was the League's Assembly so slow to reach decisions?
cards.answer: Every decision needed unanimous agreement, so a single disagreeing member could block any action from being taken.

cards.front: Why was the League seen as a 'winners' club' in its early years?
cards.answer: Germany and the USSR were both kept out at first, leaving two major world powers outside the organisation.

cards.front: What five specialist bodies carried out the League's humanitarian work in the 1920s?
cards.answer: Refugee Commission / Health Organisation / International Labour Organisation / Slavery Commission / Opium Board

cards.front: What three disputes did the League successfully resolve in the early 1920s?
cards.answer: Åland Islands (Sweden v Finland) / Upper Silesia (Germany v Poland) / Bulgaria (Greek invasion)

cards.front: Why couldn't the League stop Mussolini over the Corfu Incident?
cards.answer: The dispute was handed to the Conference of Ambassadors, a separate body of major powers, which sided with Italy instead.

cards.front: Why did the ILO's 1919 attempt to ban child labour under 14 largely fail?
cards.answer: Most member states simply ignored the ban, showing the League had no real power to enforce its own labour standards.

cards.front: What six events make up this lesson's timeline from optimism to collapse, 1924 to 1933?
cards.answer: Dawes Plan (1924) / Locarno Treaties (Oct 1925) / Germany joins the League (Sept 1926) / Kellogg-Briand Pact (Aug 1928) / Disarmament Conference begins (1932) / Germany leaves the League (Oct 1933)

cards.front: Why did the 1924 Dawes Plan leave Germany's economy vulnerable in the long run?
cards.answer: It made Germany's recovery entirely dependent on American loans, a weakness that proved disastrous once the Great Depression hit.

cards.front: Why did the USA signing the Kellogg-Briand Pact raise doubts about the League of Nations?
cards.answer: It showed the most important diplomacy of the era was happening outside Geneva, questioning what purpose the League actually served.

cards.front: What three global impacts does this lesson give for the Great Depression?
cards.answer: Trade collapsed / Mass unemployment hit every economy / Rise of extremism

cards.front: Why did Japan see the League's criticism of its actions in Manchuria as hypocritical?
cards.answer: Britain and France already had huge empires of their own, so Japan felt it unfair to be blocked from building its own.

cards.front: Why was the League's investigation into the Manchurian Crisis so slow?
cards.answer: The Lytton Commission travelled to China by boat and took over a year to report, by which time Japan controlled Manchuria.

cards.front: What three ways does this lesson say the League's sanctions on Italy were deliberately weak?
cards.answer: Oil, coal and steel were excluded / The Suez Canal stayed open to Italian ships / Non-League members like the USA kept trading
items: Oil, coal and steel were excluded
The Suez Canal stayed open to Italian ships
Non-League members like the USA kept trading

cards.front: Why did Britain and France refuse to take strong action against Italy over Abyssinia?
cards.answer: They wanted to keep Mussolini as an ally against the growing threat from Hitler's Germany, so they chose self-interest instead.

cards.front: Why did the leaked Hoare-Laval Pact cause such public outrage?
cards.answer: It revealed the League's own leading members secretly trying to reward an aggressor by carving up a fellow member state.

cards.front: What five steps did Hitler take to test the post-war settlement between 1933 and 1935?
cards.answer: Withdrawal from the League (Oct 1933) / Non-Aggression Pact with Poland (Jan 1934) / Failed Anschluss with Austria (Jul 1934) / Saar Plebiscite (Jan 1935) / Rearmament and conscription announced (Mar 1935)

cards.front: What four foreign policy aims did Hitler set out in Mein Kampf?
cards.answer: Abolish the Treaty of Versailles / Gain Lebensraum in Eastern Europe / Unite all German speakers / Defeat Communism

cards.front: Why did Britain sign the Anglo-German Naval Agreement without consulting its allies?
cards.answer: Britain believed German rearmament was happening anyway, so it judged it better to limit it through an agreement of its own.

cards.front: Why did Hitler's approach follow a pattern of probing, retreating and then advancing?
cards.answer: He tested the Allies at each stage, retreating when resisted (as over Austria in 1934) and advancing when unchallenged, making each gamble easier.

cards.front: What four critical consequences does this lesson give for the Rhineland remilitarisation?
cards.answer: Hitler's prestige soared at home / The Treaty of Versailles was effectively dead / Strategic disaster for France / Hitler and Mussolini drew closer
items: The Treaty of Versailles was effectively dead

cards.front: Which three parties failed to stop the 1936 Rhineland remilitarisation, according to this lesson?
cards.answer: France / Britain / The League of Nations

cards.front: Why didn't France act alone against the Rhineland remilitarisation despite having enough troops?
cards.answer: France was in political crisis and refused to act without British support, so when Britain said no, France did nothing.

cards.front: Why was Hitler's excuse for remilitarising the Rhineland weaker than his usual argument?
cards.answer: Germany had freely signed the Locarno Treaties accepting the demilitarised zone, so Hitler could not claim he was overturning an unfair Diktat.

cards.front: What six reasons does this lesson give for Britain following appeasement?
cards.answer: Fear of another war / The Treaty was seen as unfair / Fear of communism / Economic problems from the Depression / American isolationism / Buying time to rearm
items: The Treaty was seen as unfair

cards.front: What four historical viewpoints on appeasement does this lesson describe?
cards.answer: Guilty Men (1940) blamed Chamberlain / A.J.P. Taylor: blunders on all sides / Revisionists: Britain was too weak to act / Counter-revisionists again blamed Chamberlain
items: A.J.P. Taylor: blunders on all sides
Revisionists: Britain was too weak to act

cards.front: Why did the 1938 Anschluss leave Czechoslovakia dangerously exposed?
cards.answer: It gave Germany control of Austria's industry and resources, and left Czechoslovakia's western provinces surrounded by Germany on three sides.

cards.front: Why did the Munich Agreement push Stalin towards a deal with Hitler?
cards.answer: Stalin was insulted at being excluded from the talks and suspected Britain and France wanted Hitler to expand eastward instead.

cards.front: What four reasons does this lesson give for why Hitler signed the Nazi-Soviet Pact?
cards.answer: A green light to invade Poland / Avoided a two-front war / Stopped an Allied-Soviet alliance forming / Gained vital resources from the USSR
items: A green light to invade Poland
Gained vital resources from the USSR

cards.front: What four reasons does this lesson give for why Stalin signed the Nazi-Soviet Pact?
cards.answer: The Red Army was badly weakened / It bought time to rearm / He could move factories to safety / He gained territory and a buffer zone
items: The Red Army was badly weakened
He could move factories to safety
He gained territory and a buffer zone

cards.front: Why did Hitler's March 1939 invasion of the rest of Czechoslovakia prove appeasement had failed?
cards.answer: The rest of Czechoslovakia was not German-speaking, proving Hitler wanted empire and conquest, not just uniting German speakers.

cards.front: Why did Stalin see Britain's 1939 approach to an alliance as unserious?
cards.answer: Britain sent a negotiator by slow boat with no power to agree anything, which Stalin took as proof of half-heartedness.

cards.front: What five events make up this lesson's timeline of the outbreak of war in 1939?
cards.answer: The Gleiwitz Incident (31 Aug) / Germany invades Poland (1 Sept) / Britain and France declare war (3 Sept) / The USSR invades eastern Poland (17 Sept) / Warsaw surrenders (27 Sept)
items: Britain and France declare war (3 Sept)
The USSR invades eastern Poland (17 Sept)

cards.front: Why was the Polish army unable to resist the German Blitzkrieg in 1939?
cards.answer: Its equipment was outdated and it still used horse-mounted cavalry, no match for German tanks and dive-bombers.

cards.front: Why did Hitler stage the Gleiwitz Incident before invading Poland?
cards.answer: He needed a manufactured excuse to claim Germany was acting in self-defence, so SS troops staged a fake Polish attack.

cards.front: What three long-term causes does this lesson identify for the outbreak of the Second World War?
cards.answer: The Treaty of Versailles / The failure of the League of Nations / The Great Depression
items: The failure of the League of Nations

cards.front: What six actions does this lesson list as agreements Hitler broke on the road to war?
cards.answer: Rearmed Germany / Remilitarised the Rhineland / Carried out Anschluss with Austria / Seized the Sudetenland / Invaded the rest of Czechoslovakia / Invaded Poland

cards.front: Why do some historians see the Great Depression as essential to Hitler's rise to power?
cards.answer: Mass unemployment and poverty created conditions extremists could exploit, and without the Depression, Hitler might have stayed a fringe figure.

cards.front: Why did the League's failures over Manchuria and Abyssinia help cause the Second World War?
cards.answer: They proved collective security was an empty promise, showing Hitler that aggression would go unpunished by the international community.

cards.front: What three experiences from her early life made Elizabeth deeply distrustful of men, according to this lesson?
cards.answer: Being assaulted by Thomas Seymour / Watching her mother's execution / Seeing her sister manipulated by Philip II
items: Seeing her sister manipulated by Philip II

cards.front: Why did Henry VIII break away from the Catholic Church?
cards.answer: The Pope refused to grant him a divorce from Catherine of Aragon, so he broke from Rome to marry Anne Boleyn.

cards.front: Why did Elizabeth deliberately delay making important decisions as queen?
cards.answer: She had learned from her family's mistakes, seeing how quick, angry decisions often led to disaster, so she took her time.

cards.front: What three Catholic elements did the 1559 Religious Settlement keep?
cards.answer: Bishops / Some church decoration / Clergy vestments

cards.front: What three Protestant elements did the 1559 Religious Settlement include?
cards.answer: Services in English / The monarch as Church leader / Clergy could marry

cards.front: Why did Elizabeth's government take a harsher line as her reign progressed?
cards.answer: As threats from Catholics and Puritans grew, her government under Walsingham moved from tolerance to much stricter enforcement.

cards.front: Why did Walsingham build such an extensive spy network to uncover Catholic plots?
cards.answer: He had witnessed the mass killing of French Protestants in Paris first-hand, making him determined to root out threats to the Queen.

cards.front: What five ways did Elizabeth use propaganda to control her image?
cards.answer: Portraits / Progresses / Performances / Royal speeches / Patronage

cards.front: What five tactics did Elizabeth use to control her Privy Council?
cards.answer: Delay / Divide and rule / Careful selection / Rewards / Punishments

cards.front: Why did Elizabeth deliberately keep her Privy Council much smaller than Mary I's had been?
cards.answer: A smaller council of about 19 advisors, instead of Mary's roughly 50, was easier for Elizabeth to control.

cards.front: Why did Elizabeth deliberately choose Privy Councillors with different viewpoints?
cards.answer: It meant she heard every side of an issue before deciding, while making sure no single faction dominated her council.

cards.front: What five reasons does this lesson give for why Elizabeth's marriage mattered so much?
cards.answer: Producing an heir / Keeping out Mary, Queen of Scots / The belief a woman ruler needed a husband / Sealing alliances / The danger of choosing wrongly
items: Keeping out Mary, Queen of Scots
The belief a woman ruler needed a husband

cards.front: What five reasons does this lesson give for why Elizabeth never married?
cards.answer: Keeping her independence / No good option available / The danger of childbirth / Past family experience / Building the 'Virgin Queen' image

cards.front: Why did Elizabeth use the possibility of marriage as a diplomatic tool for so long?
cards.answer: By keeping foreign suitors interested without ever committing, she played rival powers off against each other for decades.

cards.front: Why would marrying Philip II of Spain have been unpopular in England?
cards.answer: He had already been married to Mary I, dragging England into Spain's wars, and he wanted to restore Catholicism across Europe.

cards.front: What five options did Elizabeth have when Mary, Queen of Scots, fled into England in 1568?
cards.answer: Help her regain the Scottish throne / Let her go to France / Send her back for trial / Execute her / Keep her prisoner
items: Help her regain the Scottish throne

cards.front: What three causes does this lesson give for the 1569 Northern Rebellion?
cards.answer: Religion: wanting to restore Catholicism / Power: resentment at the Council of the North / Money: Earls had lost land and mines
items: Power: resentment at the Council of the North
Money: Earls had lost land and mines

cards.front: Why did Elizabeth refuse to execute Mary, Queen of Scots, for almost two decades?
cards.answer: She feared setting a dangerous precedent by killing a fellow monarch, risking war with France or Spain, without clear proof of guilt.

cards.front: Why did the 1569 Northern Rebellion ultimately fail?
cards.answer: No foreign help arrived, many northern gentry refused to join, and a royal army far outnumbered the rebels.

cards.front: What three things did the 1570 papal bull declare about Elizabeth?
cards.answer: She was a heretic and illegitimate / Catholics need not obey her / Not a sin to plot against her
items: She was a heretic and illegitimate
Not a sin to plot against her

cards.front: What four steps made up Ridolfi's 1571 plot?
cards.answer: Assassinate Elizabeth / Replace her with Mary, Queen of Scots / Have Mary marry the Duke of Norfolk / Bring a Spanish invasion force
items: Replace her with Mary, Queen of Scots
Have Mary marry the Duke of Norfolk

cards.front: Why did the 1570 papal bull make life far more dangerous for ordinary English Catholics?
cards.answer: Before it, most Catholics were loyal subjects; afterwards, every Catholic was treated as a potential traitor, forced to choose between queen and God.

cards.front: Why did the Babington Plot finally seal Mary, Queen of Scots' fate?
cards.answer: Walsingham's code-breaker cracked a letter in which Mary appeared to approve Elizabeth's assassination, giving him the proof he needed.

cards.front: What three areas of complaint did Puritans have with the Church of England?
cards.answer: The Religious Settlement kept Catholic features / Dislike of bishops' power (hierarchy) / Objections to services and practices
items: The Religious Settlement kept Catholic features

cards.front: What four ways did Puritans express their opposition to the Church of England?
cards.answer: Pushing for reform in Parliament / Preaching and 'prophesyings' / Pamphlets and writings / Refusing to conform (vestments)

cards.front: Why did Elizabeth punish the pamphleteer John Stubbs so severely?
cards.answer: He publicly attacked her proposed marriage to a Catholic prince, so she had his hand chopped off as a warning to critics.

cards.front: Why did Elizabeth's government eventually ban 'prophesyings'?
cards.answer: These clergy meetings to discuss the Bible sometimes became forums for criticising the Church of England, so they were banned.

cards.front: What five interconnected causes led to war between England and Spain by 1588?
cards.answer: Religion / The Dutch revolt / Privateering / Catholic plots / Mary, Queen of Scots' execution

cards.front: Why did the 1585 Treaty of Nonsuch effectively mean war with Spain?
cards.answer: By openly sending troops and money to Spain's Dutch rebels, Elizabeth was effectively declaring war, and Philip saw it as aggression.

cards.front: Why did Mary, Queen of Scots' execution give Philip II a personal reason for revenge?
cards.answer: It removed the Catholic claimant he had hoped to put on the English throne, turning his cause into a personal grievance.

cards.front: What five reasons does this lesson give for why Philip II launched the Armada?
cards.answer: Religion / Political provocation (Treaty of Nonsuch) / Drake's raid on Cadiz / Mary, Queen of Scots' execution / English privateering

cards.front: What five Spanish weaknesses and mistakes does this lesson identify in the Armada campaign?
cards.answer: Medina Sidonia had no naval experience / Poor coordination with Parma's army / Many cannons had wrong-sized cannonballs / Parma's army was blockaded by Dutch ships / Missed the chance to attack England in port
items: Medina Sidonia had no naval experience
Parma's army was blockaded by Dutch ships
Missed the chance to attack England in port

cards.front: Why couldn't the Duke of Parma's army join up with the Armada as planned?
cards.answer: His barges were blockaded by Dutch rebel ships, so his invasion force could not reach the fleet off Calais.

cards.front: Why were English ships able to outfight the larger Spanish fleet?
cards.answer: English galleons were faster and easier to steer, and their cannons could be reloaded far more quickly than Spanish guns.

cards.front: What four punishments does this lesson list for the idle poor in Elizabethan England?
cards.answer: Whipping / Branding / Boring / Hanging

cards.front: What five weaknesses does this lesson identify in the Elizabethan Poor Laws?
cards.answer: Relief was often barely enough to live on / Houses of Correction were deliberately harsh / Laws didn't fix root causes like enclosure / Enforcement varied hugely between parishes / Punishments were cruel and often ineffective
items: Relief was often barely enough to live on
Houses of Correction were deliberately harsh
Laws didn't fix root causes like enclosure
Punishments were cruel and often ineffective

cards.front: Why were 'sturdy beggars' so widely feared in Elizabethan England?
cards.answer: People believed they spread plague, committed crimes and might cause rebellion, and cheap pamphlets spread panic about them further.

cards.front: Why is the 1601 Poor Law seen as such an important turning point?
cards.answer: It established that the wealthy should be taxed to fund poor relief, making poverty a government responsibility rather than private charity.

cards.front: What five motives does this lesson give for Elizabethan exploration?
cards.answer: Wealth and trade / Challenging Spain / Religion / Collapse of the wool trade / Adventure

cards.front: What six factors made Elizabethan exploration possible, according to this lesson?
cards.answer: Better ships / Rapid-fire cannons / Improved navigation / Royal support / Privateering licences / Geographical advantage

cards.front: Why does this lesson describe John Hawkins's voyages as having a 'darker legacy'?
cards.answer: His slaving voyages marked the start of English involvement in the transatlantic slave trade, which caused centuries of suffering.

cards.front: Why do historians think the Roanoke colonists disappeared in the late 1580s?
cards.answer: Historians think they either starved, were killed, or were absorbed into the local Croatoan tribe, based on the clue left behind.

title: The Rise of the Gentry & Theatre

cards.front: What four ways does this lesson give for how the wealthy displayed their status?
cards.answer: Grand houses / Fashionable clothing / Libraries and books / Sponsoring plays and entertainment

cards.front: What six reasons does this lesson give for why Elizabethan theatre flourished?
cards.answer: Clever playwrights / Court patronage / Government approval / Distraction for the poor / Growing wealth / Purpose-built theatres

cards.front: Why did Elizabeth's government see value in theatre as propaganda?
cards.answer: Plays like Shakespeare's Richard III showed the Tudors as heroes and their enemies as villains, reinforcing the social hierarchy.

cards.front: Why did Elizabeth give top government jobs to gentry men like Cecil and Walsingham rather than nobles?
cards.answer: The Tudors had a weak claim to the crown, so Elizabeth worried nobles might challenge her and preferred loyal gentry instead.

cards.front: What four reasons does this lesson give for why the Essex Rebellion failed?
cards.answer: No popular support in London / Strong, fast government response / Poor planning by Essex / Continued loyalty to Elizabeth

cards.front: What three actions did Elizabeth take against Essex after his Irish failure?
cards.answer: Placed him under house arrest / Banned him from court / Took away his wine monopoly

cards.front: Why did losing his wine monopoly push Essex towards rebellion?
cards.answer: It was his main source of income, so losing it left him deeply in debt and desperate enough to consider force.

cards.front: Why did Essex's actions in Ireland make Elizabeth furious?
cards.answer: Instead of fighting the rebellion, he wasted money, made an unauthorised truce, and returned to England without orders.

cards.front: What six methods does this lesson list for how Elizabeth dealt with the threats to her rule?
cards.answer: Walsingham's spy network / Harsh anti-Catholic laws / Mary's execution (1587) / Investment in the navy / The Religious Settlement / Control of Parliament

cards.front: What five threats to her rule does this lesson identify across Elizabeth's reign?
cards.answer: The Catholic threat / Mary, Queen of Scots / Spain / The Puritan challenge / The succession crisis

cards.front: Why does this lesson see Mary, Queen of Scots, as connecting all the Catholic threats to Elizabeth?
cards.answer: Without Mary, Catholic plotters had no realistic candidate to replace Elizabeth, so she was the figurehead every plot needed.

cards.front: Why was Spain considered the only threat with the real power to invade England?
cards.answer: Spain alone had the wealth and military strength to assemble a huge invasion fleet, unlike Catholic plotters or Puritans.

cards.front: What six pieces of evidence does this lesson give FOR Elizabeth's reign being a 'Golden Age'?
cards.answer: Cultural achievement (theatre, literature) / Exploration and naval achievement / Growing prosperity for some / Architecture and the Great Rebuilding / Relative religious stability / National pride and identity

cards.front: What six pieces of evidence does this lesson give AGAINST Elizabeth's reign being a 'Golden Age'?
cards.answer: Widespread poverty and inequality / Religious persecution / Ongoing threats and conflict / The slave trade / Limited rights and opportunities / Propaganda and image control

cards.front: Why does this lesson argue the 'Golden Age' benefited some groups far more than others?
cards.answer: It was a Golden Age for the gentry, merchants and culturally privileged, but not for the majority, who faced poverty and hardship.

cards.front: Why did the government see theatre as a useful distraction for the poor?
cards.answer: Not everyone was getting richer, and the government felt entertainment like theatre would keep people occupied and make rebellion less likely.

cards.front: What four environments structure this lesson's account of the Armada campaign?
cards.answer: The Channel / Calais anchorage / Gravelines / The north-about route home

cards.front: Why couldn't the Armada restock supplies during the week-long Channel fight?
cards.answer: Every port along that coast was English, so Howard's fleet could resupply while the Spanish had no friendly port at all.

cards.front: Why did the Armada anchor in the exposed roadstead off Calais rather than a proper harbour?
cards.answer: Spain controlled no deep-water port there, and Parma's barges were blockaded behind sandbanks, leaving the open roadstead as the only option.

cards.front: What four building works did Leicester carry out at Kenilworth for Elizabeth's visits?
cards.answer: Leicester's Building (state apartments) / A new gatehouse / Great windows cut into the Norman keep / A privy garden with terraces and a fountain
items: Great windows cut into the Norman keep
A privy garden with terraces and a fountain

cards.front: What entertainments filled Elizabeth's nineteen days at Kenilworth in 1575?
cards.answer: Hunting in the chase / Masques and dancing / Bear-baiting / An Italian acrobat / A rustic wedding / Spectacular fireworks

cards.front: Why did Leicester design such an elaborate arrival pageant for Elizabeth in 1575?
cards.answer: The staging argued that the castle, its host and all its magnificence existed for Elizabeth alone, pressing his case to marry her.

cards.front: Why do historians think Elizabeth declined the final planned entertainment at Kenilworth?
cards.answer: One more entertainment on the marriage theme was prepared but never performed, seen by many historians as her refusing to be lectured.

cards.front: What are the Four Humours and their linked seasons, according to Hippocrates?
cards.answer: Blood – spring, air, hot and wet / Yellow Bile – summer, fire, hot and dry / Black Bile – autumn, earth, cold and dry / Phlegm – winter, water, cold and wet
items: Blood – spring, air, hot and wet
Yellow Bile – summer, fire, hot and dry
Black Bile – autumn, earth, cold and dry
Phlegm – winter, water, cold and wet

cards.front: What treatment did Galen prescribe for an excess of each of the Four Humours?
cards.answer: Too much blood – bleeding / Too much yellow bile – vomiting (emetics) / Too much black bile – purging (laxatives) / Too much phlegm – warming and sweating
items: Too much phlegm – warming and sweating

cards.front: Why couldn't anyone check whether Galen's anatomical descriptions were accurate for centuries?
cards.answer: The Church banned human dissection for most of the medieval period, so nobody could test his often-inaccurate, animal-based descriptions.

cards.front: Why did medieval physicians consult zodiac charts before treating patients?
cards.answer: They believed the stars and planets affected the balance of the humours, so treatment timing depended on a favourable position.

cards.front: What five features does this lesson give of medieval hospitals?
cards.answer: Run by monks, nuns or religious orders / Provided food, shelter, warmth and prayer / Rarely attempted to treat or cure disease / Often refused patients with infectious disease / Focused on spiritual care, not medicine
items: Run by monks, nuns or religious orders
Provided food, shelter, warmth and prayer
Rarely attempted to treat or cure disease
Often refused patients with infectious disease
Focused on spiritual care, not medicine

cards.front: What four reasons does this lesson give for why Islamic medicine advanced while Europe stagnated?
cards.answer: Religious encouragement to seek knowledge / Wealth and stability funded learning / A movement to translate and expand texts / A practical emphasis on observation
items: A movement to translate and expand texts

cards.front: Why was Roger Bacon imprisoned by the Church?
cards.answer: He argued doctors should experiment rather than simply follow Galen, directly challenging Church teaching, so he was arrested as a warning.

cards.front: Why were monasteries much cleaner and healthier than medieval towns?
cards.answer: Monks had the wealth, knowledge and discipline to build proper water supplies and latrines, unlike most towns.

cards.front: What three great problems made medieval surgery so dangerous?
cards.answer: Pain / Infection / Bleeding

cards.front: What five procedures could medieval barber surgeons perform, according to this lesson?
cards.answer: Amputation / Trepanning / Setting broken bones / Cauterisation / Pulling teeth

cards.front: Why did medieval surgeons often fail to prevent infection in wounds?
cards.answer: Many believed pus in a wound, 'laudable pus', was a good sign of healing, when it was actually a sign of infection.

cards.front: Why did warfare help drive improvements in medieval surgical skill?
cards.answer: Most barber surgeons gained their experience treating battlefield wounds, and decades of war created constant demand for better treatment.

cards.front: What four public health problems did medieval towns face, according to this lesson?
cards.answer: Waste in the streets / Contaminated water supplies / Overcrowding / Animals kept within town walls

cards.front: What six ways did people try to prevent or treat the Black Death?
cards.answer: Flagellants whipping themselves / Carrying posies and herbs / Bloodletting and purging / Quarantine of infected houses / Prayer and processions / Fires and ringing bells

cards.front: Why did the Black Death shift power from landowners towards peasants?
cards.answer: So many people died that surviving peasants became scarce, letting them demand higher wages or leave for better-paid work.

cards.front: Why might killing stray dogs and cats during the Great Plague of 1665 have made things worse?
cards.answer: It ironically removed some of the very creatures — cats and dogs — that preyed on the plague-carrying rats.

cards.front: Why couldn't Harvey explain how blood passed from arteries into veins?
cards.answer: Microscopes of his time were too weak to reveal capillaries, the tiny vessels that complete the circuit, until decades later.

cards.front: Why was Paré's discovery of his wound-healing balm significant?
cards.answer: He ran out of cauterising oil and improvised a soothing cream instead, which healed wounds better and with far less pain.

cards.front: What three old beliefs about disease persisted into the 18th century, according to this lesson?
cards.answer: Miasma ('bad air') / The Four Humours / Illness as God's punishment

cards.front: What four types of medical practitioner could ordinary people visit in the 1600s–1700s?
cards.answer: Barber-surgeons / Apothecaries / Wise women / Quack doctors

cards.front: Why was getting bodies for dissection such a major problem for surgeons like Hunter?
cards.answer: Henry VIII had granted surgeons only 4 hanged criminals a year, hopelessly inadequate as demand grew, so stolen corpses were traded instead.

cards.front: Why is John Hunter's treatment of the popliteal aneurysm seen as an important example of his method?
cards.answer: Instead of amputating, he tied off the artery higher up and let other vessels expand, showing his method of observe, test, solve.

cards.front: What three problems did this lesson identify with inoculation before Jenner's vaccine?
cards.answer: It was a huge gamble / Inoculated people could spread the disease / It was expensive
items: Inoculated people could spread the disease

cards.front: What five reasons does this lesson give for opposition to Jenner's vaccination?
cards.answer: Religious objections / Mistrust from doctors who lost income / Jenner couldn't explain the mechanism / Fear and misinformation (cartoons) / Organised opposition (Anti-Vaccination League)
items: Mistrust from doctors who lost income

cards.front: Why couldn't Jenner explain why his vaccine actually worked?
cards.answer: He had observed its effects through experiment but could not describe the biological mechanism, since Germ Theory came decades later.

cards.front: Why did some doctors oppose Jenner's vaccination even though it was safer?
cards.answer: Vaccination threatened the income of doctors who earned a living performing the older, more expensive method of inoculation.

title: The Germ Theory: Pasteur and Koch

cards.front: What three claims made up Pasteur's 1861 Germ Theory?
cards.answer: Germs are present in the air / Germs cause decay / The same germs could cause disease in humans
items: Germs are present in the air
The same germs could cause disease in humans

cards.front: What four techniques did Koch develop for studying bacteria?
cards.answer: Growing bacteria on agar jelly / Staining bacteria with dyes / Photographing bacteria under the microscope / Proving infection using animal experiments

cards.front: Why did Pasteur's swan-necked flask experiment disprove spontaneous generation?
cards.answer: The curved neck let air in but trapped airborne microbes, so the broth stayed fresh until the neck was broken and germs got in.

cards.front: Why did the rivalry between Pasteur and Koch actually speed up medical progress?
cards.answer: National competition pushed each to try to outdo the other in identifying germs and developing vaccines, accelerating discoveries.

cards.front: What three barriers to safe surgery does this lesson identify?
cards.answer: Pain / Infection / Blood loss

cards.front: What four reasons does this lesson give for surgeons' opposition to Lister's antiseptic methods?
cards.answer: The carbolic spray was unpleasant to use / Some doubted it really killed germs / Public criticism from Charlton Bastian / His methods were hard to replicate
items: The carbolic spray was unpleasant to use
Some doubted it really killed germs
His methods were hard to replicate

cards.front: Why did surgical death rates rise during the 'Black Period' after anaesthetics were introduced?
cards.answer: With patients unconscious, surgeons attempted longer, deeper operations, but without antiseptics this exposed them to far greater infection risk.

cards.front: Why was Queen Victoria's use of chloroform in 1853 such an important turning point?
cards.answer: Her public endorsement silenced much religious criticism and made anaesthetics socially acceptable for widespread use.

cards.front: What five factors combined to end laissez-faire in public health, according to this lesson?
cards.answer: Chadwick's statistics on filth and disease / Snow's proof cholera spread by water / Pasteur's Germ Theory (1861) / The Great Stink of 1858 / The 1867 Reform Act widening the vote
items: Chadwick's statistics on filth and disease
Snow's proof cholera spread by water
The 1867 Reform Act widening the vote

cards.front: Why were John Snow's findings on cholera initially rejected by many doctors?
cards.answer: He could prove contaminated water caused cholera but could not explain why without knowledge of germs, so many kept believing in miasma.

cards.front: Why was the 1875 Public Health Act so much more effective than the 1848 Act?
cards.answer: Unlike the voluntary 1848 Act, the 1875 Act was compulsory, forcing every council to act and leaving no room for inaction.

cards.front: What five factors does this lesson identify in the development of penicillin?
cards.answer: Chance (the mould contamination) / Individual genius (Fleming, Florey, Chain) / Science and technology / War (WWII urgency) / Government investment

cards.front: What three named steps does this lesson use to structure the development of penicillin?
cards.answer: Step 1: Fleming's chance discovery / Step 2: Florey and Chain's breakthrough / Step 3: Mass production through war and government
items: Step 3: Mass production through war and government

cards.front: Why does this lesson argue Fleming's discovery of penicillin was more than just luck?
cards.answer: Although the mould landing on his dish was chance, his scientific expertise let him recognise its importance rather than discard it.

cards.front: Why did Albert Alexander's case in 1941 prove the urgent need for mass production of penicillin?
cards.answer: Penicillin began curing him, but the tiny supply ran out after five days, so he relapsed and died, proving the need for scale.

cards.front: What were Beveridge's Five Giants that the welfare state had to defeat?
cards.answer: Want (poverty) / Disease (lack of healthcare) / Ignorance (poor education) / Squalor (bad housing) / Idleness (unemployment)

cards.front: What six Liberal Reforms does this lesson list between 1906 and 1911?
cards.answer: School Meals Act (1906) / School Medical Inspections (1907) / Children's Charter (1908) / Old Age Pensions Act (1908) / Labour Exchanges (1909) / National Insurance Act (1911)

cards.front: Why did Booth's and Rowntree's surveys undermine the Victorian belief that poverty was caused by laziness?
cards.answer: Their statistics showed poverty was widespread and caused by low wages, illness, old age and unemployment, not personal failings.

cards.front: Why did the Boer War push the British government towards welfare reform?
cards.answer: Around 40% of volunteers from industrial cities were too unhealthy to serve, becoming a national embarrassment and a security threat.

cards.front: What are the three core principles of the NHS, according to this lesson?
cards.answer: Universal / Comprehensive / Free at the point of delivery
items: Free at the point of delivery

cards.front: What four types of healthcare did this lesson say existed before the NHS in 1948?
cards.answer: Private doctors (for the wealthy) / Voluntary hospitals (for charity cases) / Council-run hospitals (former workhouses) / The 'panel system' under National Insurance

cards.front: Why did most doctors eventually agree to join the NHS despite fierce initial opposition?
cards.answer: Bevan split the profession, offering consultants generous salaries and continued private practice, which isolated and broke the BMA's resistance.

cards.front: Why did the Emergency Medical Service of 1939 matter for the creation of the NHS?
cards.answer: It proved a state-run system coordinating hospitals nationally could work, while also exposing how unequal healthcare had been.

cards.front: What three reasons does this lesson give for why war accelerates medical progress?
cards.answer: It creates urgency / It provides funding / It offers a testing ground

cards.front: What three areas of modern surgical technology does this lesson describe?
cards.answer: Transplant surgery / Keyhole and robotic surgery / Scanning technology (CT and MRI)

cards.front: Why did Florence Nightingale's use of statistics matter as much as her nursing reforms?
cards.answer: She used statistics, including her 'coxcomb' diagrams, to prove most deaths were caused by preventable disease, not battle wounds.

cards.front: Why did keyhole surgery represent such a major advance over traditional open surgery?
cards.answer: Small cuts and tiny cameras replaced large incisions, meaning less pain, smaller scars and much faster recovery for patients.

cards.front: What three long-term degenerative conditions does this lesson name as major modern health challenges?
cards.answer: Cancer / Alzheimer's disease / Parkinson's disease

cards.front: What three lifestyle diseases does this lesson link to modern diet and habits?
cards.answer: Type 2 diabetes / Heart disease / Some cancers (lung, liver, bowel)

cards.front: Why has antibiotic resistance become such a serious modern problem?
cards.answer: Decades of overusing antibiotics in medicine and farming let bacteria evolve resistance, while drug companies invested less in new ones.

cards.front: Why did Andrew Wakefield's fraudulent 1998 MMR study cause lasting harm even after being discredited?
cards.answer: Vaccination rates had already dropped, so measles, once almost eliminated, began to return, showing progress can be undone by lost trust.
